markdownRemark.html:
In startup world, I think there are 2 styles.

One is Silicon Valley style. You put everything into one idea for a long time. You stay with it. You build through pain. You keep going even when results are slow.

The other is Hollywood style. More project-based. New idea, new team, new hype, then next one. Fast move. Fast learning. Fast switch.

Neither is totally right or wrong. Both can create great things. But they make very different engineers.

When I look at my own path, I was mostly Hollywood style. I worked on 3 cool companies/startups/projects so far, and I was usually the person who jumped into the next challenge. From outside, it looked exciting. Always something new. Always a new story.

At the beginning of my career, that was perfect for me. I was hungry. I wanted new tech, new challenge, new environment. I wanted to prove that I can survive anywhere. So I kept choosing hard things and moving fast.

But now I can’t leave one idea so simply anymore. Something changed inside me.

Recently I looked back and asked myself: what the heck did I actually do?

I fought many challenges, yes. But fought for what?

Career growth? More income? Ego?

Did I enjoy it? Yeah, I did. But if I’m brutally honest, sometimes I enjoyed "me" in that story more than the mission itself.

I liked being the person who can jump into anything. I liked feeling proud. I liked saying, “I can do this too.”

But did I deeply love every idea? Not always. And that question is getting louder as I grow.

Now I want something more real. I want to work on something I truly care about. Not just interesting. Not just trendy. Not just good for resume.

So maybe this is the next chapter for me: less Hollywood switching, more Silicon Valley commitment. Not because one style is cooler, but because now I want to build deeper, not just faster.

I want to stay with one idea long enough to see who I become while building it.

If I can keep that startup fire and still not run away when it gets hard, boring, slow, and messy, then maybe I can finally call myself a real startup-type engineer.

frontmatter.title: Am I Really a Startup Engineer?
frontmatter.description: Looking back at my first startup years and asking what I really want to build
